title: Young Goodman Brown
focus: the loss of faith in human goodness

teacherSummary.text: In Puritan Salem, Goodman Brown leaves his new wife Faith for a night errand in the forest, where he walks with a traveler resembling his own grandfather, carrying a serpent-like staff. He sees pious townspeople, his minister and finally Faith herself gathering for a witches' communion. He cries out for Faith to resist and finds himself alone. Whether dream or not, he lives out his life gloomy and distrustful, and 'his dying hour was gloom.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Young Goodman Brown,” how does Hawthorne show the loss of faith in human goodness? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the allusion you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Young Goodman Brown, how does Hawthorne develop the idea of the loss of faith in human goodness? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the allusion in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Young Goodman Brown develops the idea of the loss of faith in human goodness. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of allusion and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Young Goodman Brown (where it begins, turns and ends) and its allusion shape the reader's understanding of the loss of faith in human goodness. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Young Goodman Brown suggests about the loss of faith in human goodness. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's allusion and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Nathaniel Hawthorne uses allusion in Young Goodman Brown to complicate the reader's understanding of the loss of faith in human goodness. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Young Goodman Brown within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the loss of faith in human goodness responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Young Goodman Brown alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the loss of faith in human goodness follows or bends those conventions, using the allusion as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Young Goodman Brown and its treatment of the loss of faith in human goodness. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's allusion and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Young Goodman Brown as evidence for a larger claim about the loss of faith in human goodness in Young Goodman Brown. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Young Goodman Brown as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the loss of faith in human goodness. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Young Goodman Brown.

satQuestions.passage: They continued to walk onward, while the elder traveller exhorted his companion to make good speed and persevere in the path, discoursing so aptly that his arguments seemed rather to spring up in the bosom of his auditor than to be suggested by himself. As they went, he plucked a branch of maple to serve for a walking stick, and began to strip it of the twigs and little boughs, which were wet with evening dew. The moment his fingers touched them they became strangely withered and dried up as with a week's sunshine. Thus the pair proceeded, at a good free pace, until suddenly, in a gloomy hollow of the road, Goodman Brown sat himself down on the stump of a tree and refused to go any farther.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Young Goodman Brown”?
options: A reversal that punishes a change of heart
The foolishness of wishing to be young again
Guilt that the mind cannot hide
The loss of faith in human goodness

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What would happen to you if you came to believe everyone you trust is secretly bad? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes witchcraft; devil figure.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are nettled, intercepted, auditor, composedly, meditate. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “considerably nettled, "there is my wife, Faith.” In this sentence it means: irritated; annoyed. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Young Goodman Brown would have known. Hawthorne (1835) was descended from John Hathorne, a judge at the 1692 Salem witch trials. Why does this story matter? An allegory central to American literature courses; in Gale's Short Stories for Students vol. 1. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for allusion.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “They continued to walk onward, while the elder traveller exhorted his companion to make good speed and persevere in the path, discoursing so aptly that his arguments seemed rather to spring up in the bosom of his auditor” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the loss of faith in human goodness? I circle “auditor”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find allusion, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for allusion.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of allusion. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: They continued to walk onward, while the elder traveller exhorted his companion to make good speed and persevere in the path, discoursing so aptly that his arguments seemed rather to spring up in the bosom of his auditor than to be suggested by himself. As they went, he plucked a branch of maple to serve for a walking stick, and began to strip it of the twigs and little boughs, which were wet with evening dew. The moment his fingers touched them they became strangely withered and dried up as with a week's sunshine. Thus the pair proceeded, at a good free pace, until suddenly, in a gloomy hollow of the road, Goodman Brown sat himself down on the stump of a tree and refused to go any farther.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Allusion, Symbolism, Setting: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Young Goodman Brown develops the idea of the loss of faith in human goodness. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of allusion and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to faith and doubt? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about the loss of faith in human goodness, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how allusion shapes the loss of faith in human goodness. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
